 Economic Indicators Shifting income patterns cut 25 years from Social Security's projected lifespan, AARP says
 The share of GDP subject to payroll tax fell to 34% in 2025 from 41% in 1984, a $10.8 trillion revenue gap through 2034, AARP says
 By Colleen Cabili · 2 min read · Updated November 11, 2026 Add QZ to Google Bloomberg / Getty Images
 AARP published a report on Tuesday concluding that shifting income patterns have cut 25 years from Social Security's projected solvency.
 Social Security's trustees project that the program's combined trust fund will run out in 2034. AARP said that had payroll tax receipts held steady against gross domestic product, the program would have brought in an extra $10.8 trillion from 1984 through 2034 and would be able to cover scheduled benefits in full through 2059.
 The share of GDP subject to the payroll tax, the program's primary income source, fell from 41% in 1984 to 34% in 2025, AARP said.
 "There is more income going to high-wage workers that is not captured by Social Security," Richard Johnson, the report's author and the AARP Public Policy Institute's vice president of financial security, said in an AARP article . Wage gains have been concentrated at the top of the income scale, and the payroll tax applies to earnings up to an annual cap. The cap is $184,500 in 2026 and will rise to $192,300 in 2027.
 Corporate profits and investment returns, which are not taxed for Social Security, have grown faster than worker compensation, AARP's analysis found. Labor income's share of GDP fell from 65% in 1970 to 57% in 2023. More business owners are structuring their companies as S corporations, which lets them claim income as profits that escape the payroll tax.
 The $10.8 trillion figure is in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars, and earnings met or exceeded the cap for 6% of individuals in 2024, according to CNBC .
 The paper does not endorse specific solutions. It cites bills before Congress that would raise or eliminate the payroll tax cap and tax investment income above a threshold, including the Social Security 2100 Act, the Social Security Expansion Act and the Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act. The Social Security 2100 Act would eliminate the cap and add a tax on investment income for taxpayers earning more than $400,000.
 Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) have proposed eliminating the cap but have not introduced legislation, according to AARP.
 Johnson said these proposals "would not affect lower- or middle-income taxpayers."
 Bill Sweeney, AARP's senior vice president for government affairs, said the findings undercut calls to raise the retirement age and cut benefits. "Social Security isn't facing insolvency because retirees are taking out too much; it happened because the economy changed and Congress never took action to keep up with it," Sweeney said.
 Johnson made a similar point at a Tuesday press briefing, according to CNBC. "The fix for Social Security isn't cutting earned benefits; it's rebuilding the revenue behind them," he said.
